title: Decarbonising industrial hydrogen supply systems under EU taxonomy regulation: A multi-objective decision-support framework for existing facilities
source: ScienceDirect Publication: Applied Energy
abstract: Hydrogen is a crucial vector for decarbonising hard-to-abate industrial sectors, but its deployment increasingly depends on regulatory sustainability criteria alongside economic performance. In Europe, frameworks such as the EU Taxonomy and RED II impose life cycle emission thresholds that directly influence hydrogen system design. This work proposes a flexible multi-objective mixed-integer linear programming framework for the design of lowcarbon hydrogen supply systems for industrial applications. The model integrates renewable and biogenic resources, electricity generation, hydrogen production technologies, inter-monthly hydrogen storage, and resource-specific transport. Economic performance and life cycle CO2eq emissions are optimised simultaneously by using an augmented epsilon-constraint method, while regulatory sustainability thresholds are assessed a posteriori. Water consumption is explicitly included, enabling analysis in regions were water scarcity constraints production. The framework is applied to western Andalusia (Spain) and the Republic of Ireland, which differ in resource availability and hydrogen demand. Regional resource-to-demand ratios strongly shape Pareto front structures and technology portfolios. Biomass gasification emerges as the most cost-effective pathway in resource-abundant settings, while electrolytic routes dominate in resource-constrained regions. All Pareto-optimal solutions comply with the EU Taxonomy emission threshold, although the economic cost of compliance differs between regions. Overall, the framework provides a transparent and adaptable decision-support tool for assessing cost-emission trade-offs and regulatory compliance in regional hydrogen planning. It supports the development of context-specific, policy-consistent hydrogen roadmaps that balance economic competitiveness, environmental performance, and sustainability requirements.

title: Distinct DNA-binding modes of Sp8 and Sp6 shape a hierarchical regulatory network in limb ectoderm
source: Biological sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: Sp8 and Sp6 are closely related transcription factors expressed in the limb ectoderm, where they control proximo-distal and dorso-ventral patterning, yet their direct targets and molecular mechanisms have remained unclear. Combining genome-wide chromatin occupancy with transcriptomic profiling in vivo, we identify shared and specific targets and reconstruct the Sp8/Sp6 gene regulatory network, establishing Sp8 as its dominant, hierarchical node. Mechanistically, the two factors diverge: Sp8 binds DNA directly at canonical GC-rich Sp motifs, regulating targets including Fgf8 and Sp6 itself, whereas Sp6 acts as a transcriptional cofactor. Via indirect binding to AT-rich motifs through Dlx, both cooperatively regulate limb-patterning pathways, including Wnt, FGF, TGF-β/BMP, and Notch. Biochemical assays confirm that both form homo- and heterodimers and interact with Dlx5 through their zinc-finger domains. Together, these findings reveal how Sp8 and Sp6 orchestrate AER formation and dorso-ventral patterning, providing a mechanistic framework for congenital limb malformations such as split-hand/foot malformation.

title: A master gene for Drosophila male courtship prevents the behavior in females via a truncated protein
source: Biological sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: Decades of studies have established that a terminal gene in the sex determination hierarchy, fruitless (fru), controls nearly all aspects of male courtship behaviors in Drosophila and many other insects. fru is transcribed in a sex-specific manner to produce male-specific Fru proteins (FruM) and was considered nonfunctional in females. In this study, we identify a female-specific truncated Fru protein (FruF) that is specifically expressed during the pupal stage and distributed in both cell bodies and neuronal projections, in contrast to FruM, which is expressed from larval to adult stages and localized to nuclei. We discover that FruF cooperates with another sex determination gene, doublesex (dsx), to prevent male-typical courtship in females. Knocking down fruF in dsx-expressing pC1 neurons induces courtship in females. These results reveal that the master gene for male courtship prevents this behavior in females via a truncated protein, thereby refining the canonical sex determination hierarchy that controls sexual development and behaviors.

title: Boosting Sensitivity of High-Dimensional Solid-State NMR of Proteins by Optimizing Coherence Transfers
source: Biological sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: TROP it or drop it: Owing to fast magic-angle spinning at frequencies above 50 kHz, solid-state nuclear magnetic resonance has evolved as a versatile method to decipher protein structure, dynamics, and chemical properties. While conceptually, higher-dimensional approaches such as 4D and 5D correlation spectra are capable of exceeding the established molecular-weight limitations by ameliorating signal overlap, their intrinsic implications for sensitivity and measurement times required have severely limited these important prospects in practice. Here we show that in high-dimensional experiments, the extensive use of dedicated transverse-mixing optimal control pulses (TROPs) can reduce the necessary measurement time by almost an order of magnitude. TROP’ed non-uniformly sampled experiments not only benefit from a multiplicative sensitivity enhancement in each complex time point due to concomitant transfer of both components of complex signals along multi-step magnetization transfer pathways, but additionally from facilitation of reconstruction with better raw data. Aided by the processing framework provided to future users here, the combination of an extensive use of TROPs with increased dimensionality hence presents itself as highly promising to ameliorate the conventional limitations of solid-state NMR.

title: Ikaros transcription factors prevent the activation of an endothelial cell program in bone marrow hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells
source: Biological sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: Hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) are generally committed to the hematopoietic lineage, but how that commitment is maintained is not well understood. We show that the Ikaros family of transcription factors is essential for HSC identity. Ikaros, alone or in combination with Helios, is required to sustain the pool of multipotent HSCs and their downstream progenitor cells in adult animals, by directly repressing a core group of genes implicated in wound healing, cell junction organization, and actin cytoskeleton organization. Remarkably, upon in vivo or in vitro deletion of Ikaros or Ikaros+Helios, nearly one-third of the hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells (HSPCs) rapidly exhibit an endothelial cell transcriptomic signature, and develop non-hematopoietic structures resembling CD144+ endothelial-like cells. These results indicate that adult HSPCs are highly plastic and prevented from activating an endothelial cell program by Ikaros family transcription factors.

title: Chromosomally unstable cancer cells exhibit heightened dependence on the mitotic SKA complex
source: Biological sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: Aneuploidy and chromosomal instability are common characteristics of cancer but remain underexploited therapeutically. Chromosomally unstable cells are often selectively vulnerable to inhibition of the kinesin KIF18A, and this dependence is related to altered mitotic control. Here, we identify the spindle and kinetochore-associated (SKA) complex as a mitotic regulator that establishes a similar dependency. SKA complex loss is tolerated in cells with a defective mitotic checkpoint, but when mitosis is prolonged, it leads to mitotic errors and loss of viability. Genetic analysis reveals that the SKA complex and KIF18A are epistatic, although they function through mechanistically distinct mitotic pathways. SKA complex depletion selectively impacts chromosomally unstable cancer cells and mirrors the effects of KIF18A inhibition. We thus identify a cellular vulnerability associated with prolonged mitosis in chromosomally unstable cancers.

title: Selective mTOR inhibition via FLCN drives TFE3-dependent VLDL-TG secretion and protects from MAFLD/MASH
source: Biological sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: Hepatic lipid homeostasis is controlled by multiple processes, including VLDL-TG secretion. We have previously shown that the FLCN/TFE3 branch of mTORC1 signaling controls hepatic fatty acid oxidation and de novo lipogenesis to protect mice from MAFLD. We now show that the FLCN/TFE3 pathway also controls VLDL-TG secretion via direct transcriptional activation of a broad program of genes involved in VLDL-TG secretion, including PCYT1A, the rate-limiting step of phosphatidylcholine synthesis. Loss of hepatic FLCN upregulates VLDL-TG secretion and prevents MAFLD, and this protection requires TFE3 and PCYT1A. The data unveil a new pathway that orchestrates multiple steps of VLDL-TG synthesis and secretion. The data also highlight that suppressing the selective FLCN/TFE3 branch of mTORC1 signaling maximizes hepatic lipid clearance by coordinately promoting fatty acid oxidation, suppressing de novo lipogenesis, and boosting VLDL-TG secretion, providing an attractive therapeutic target for the treatment of MAFLD.

title: N–Atom Transfer Reactivity of Terminal Cobalt Nitrides
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract We report the photogeneration and characterization of four-coordinate terminal cobalt nitrides (EmL)Co(N)(L) (L = pyridine, 4-dimethylaminopyridine) using a sterically encumbered dipyrrin ligand environment. The photolytic generation of the terminal nitride complexes were achieved in both the crystalline state and in frozen solution matrices to determine its molecular (single-crystal X-ray diffraction) and electronic structures (EPR). The solid-state structure, EPR spectrum, and computational analysis support a doublet ground state (S = 1/2) arising from antiferromagnetic coupling between high-spin CoII and a triplet nitride (3N–). Notably, the elongated Co–N bond distance (1.74(3) Å) suggests an attenuated π-interaction between the Co–N pair, consistent with the significant nitride-centered radical character. The electronic structure engenders unusual reactivity including (i) H2 cleavage, (ii) aromatic aryl ring expansion, and (iii) N–atom insertion into C(sp2)–C(sp2) bonds. The observed reactivity profile broadens our fundamental understanding of metal nitride chemistry as well as establishes a foundation for developing N–atom transfer reactions from formally high-valent metal nitrides.

title: Humidity-Regulated MOF-Kirigami Passive Flyer
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract While passive flyers have gained increasing attention as an energy-efficient alternative to active unmanned aerial vehicles, they are challenged by limited flight time, high energy consumption, and large-scale deployment issues caused by heavy batteries and complex electronics. The dandelion seed, a natural passive flyer for wind-borne dispersal, has inspired the design of synthetic biomimetic counterparts that similarly leverage airflow for sustained locomotion. However, existing designs lack adaptive mechanisms to respond to diverse environmental conditions such as humidity variation, limiting their functionality in real-world atmospheres. Thus, a humidity-regulated passive flyer was presented here which integrates a ZPF-2-Co metal-organic framework (MOF)-polymer composite humidity actuator into a dandelion-seed-inspired kirigami structure. This flyer is capable of altering its flight position based on ambient humidity, enabling adaptive dispersal. A theoretical model about descent of a dandelion seed was established, using fluid dynamics simulations to analyze the flow field and pressure distribution. It is revealed that a vortex ring formed above the pappus increases drag and slows descent, while a restoring torque stabilizes the attitude and enables gliding upon tilt. Flight tests under seven humidity conditions reveal that the flyer descends vertically below 70% RH, transitions into stable gliding between 70% and 80% RH for controlled long-distance dispersal, and loses gliding stability due to flipping when RH exceeds 84.6%. The passive flyers developed in this work validate the humidity-regulating functionality of MOFs and their potential implementation in flexible devices, providing a foundation for future applications such as smart agriculture, distributed environmental sensing, and pollution tracking.

title: Ultrastretchable Liquid-Metal Reinforced Polyelectrolyte Hydrogel Sensors for Multichannel Gesture Recognition and Robotic-Hand Control
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract With the development of wearable devices, human-motion monitoring, and human–machine interaction technologies, flexible sensing materials with high stretchability, rapid response, high sensitivity, and cyclic stability are increasingly required. To address conductive-pathway instability under large and repeated deformation, interfacial failure associated with layered liquid-metal/hydrogel architectures, and the difficulty in balancing mechanical deformability with sensing performance, this work reports a liquid-metal-reinforced polyelectrolyte hydrogel based on (2-(acryloyloxy)ethyl)trimethylammonium chloride (AETC) and eutectic gallium–indium (EGaIn) microdroplets. EGaIn was ultrasonically dispersed in water, introduced into an aqueous AETC precursor, and immobilized within the poly(AETC) network through UV-induced radical polymerization, yielding a bulk-dispersed AETC@LM hydrogel, where AETC@LM denotes an AETC-derived polyelectrolyte hydrogel containing dispersed EGaIn microdroplets. The effects of liquid-metal content on the morphology, chemical structure, mechanical properties, water retention, adhesion, and electromechanical sensing performance of the hydrogels were systematically investigated. Among the investigated formulations, LM200, prepared with 200 μL of the liquid-metal dispersion, exhibited the most favorable overall performance. It sustained a maximum tensile strain of approximately 3000% and provided strain sensing over 0–900%. Piecewise least-squares linear fitting of the strain response yielded gauge factors of 1.4 and 11.3 in the low- and high-strain regions, respectively. Similarly, piecewise least-squares linear fitting of the pressure response yielded sensitivities of 8.07 kPa–1 over approximately 0–7 kPa and 0.68 kPa–1 over approximately 8–25 kPa. LM200 retained approximately 95% of its initial mass after four weeks of ambient storage and exhibited adhesion to different substrates, with the highest adhesion strength observed on wood. The sensor showed response and recovery times of 0.24 and 0.18 s, respectively, and maintained repeatable resistance responses over 600 tensile cycles at 50% strain. Furthermore, five LM200 sensors were integrated into a five-channel smart glove. A ResNet50-based residual-learning model classified ten representative gestures from the acquired multichannel signals, which were also mapped to corresponding robotic-hand postures. The principal innovation of this work is the material-to-system integration of a bulk-dispersed liquid-metal/AETC polyelectrolyte architecture with strain–pressure dual-mode sensing and machine-learning-assisted multichannel gesture recognition. This integrated strategy establishes a structure–property–application relationship for liquid-metal-reinforced polyelectrolyte hydrogels and provides an experimental basis for large-deformation wearable sensing and intelligent human–machine interaction.

title: Redox-Active Self-Assembled Monolayers Drive Actuation in Hierarchical Nanoporous Gold
source: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Hierarchical nanoporous metals derived from dealloying offer lightweight, high-surface-area architectures with considerable promise for catalysis, energy storage, actuation, and sensing. Yet, the extent to which structural hierarchy and surface functionalization govern the functional properties of these materials remains largely unexplored. Here, we demonstrate reversible potential-induced actuation in millimeter-sized hierarchical nanoporous gold functionalized with ferrocene-terminated alkanethiol self-assembled monolayers (Fc-SAMs). In situ dilatometry in aqueous electrolyte reveals that redox conversion of the ferrocene headgroups generates pronounced mechanical deformation. Relative to a single-pore-size material, hierarchical nanoporous gold exhibits markedly larger strain amplitudes, consistent with its increased surface area and higher Fc-SAM coverage. Strikingly, the relationship between actuation strain and charge exhibits a quadratic dependence, in contrast to the linear behavior reported for earlier electrochemical actuators based on nanoporous gold. This finding highlights the significant role of the conformational dynamics of soft-matter SAMs in governing the mechanical response of metallic nanomaterials. In addition, the hierarchical material displays faster charging kinetics, supporting the notion that ion accessibility and mass transport are enhanced within the multiscale pore network. These results establish hierarchical nanoporous metals as a promising platform for chemo-mechanical sensing, in which chemical reactions at functionalized surfaces are directly transduced into measurable mechanical signals.

title: GTP hydrolysis by Ras proceeds without a stabilized nucleophilic water molecule
source: Biological sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: A comprehensive understanding of the Ras self-inactivation mechanism at atomic resolution—specifically, intrinsic GTP hydrolysis converting the GTP-bound active form to the GDP-bound inactive form—is essential for designing therapies against Ras-driven cancers. Conventional models describe a biphasic GTP-bound state: Ras interconverts between inactive state 1 and active, catalytically competent state 2. However, the structural pathway leading to Ras/GDP via these states remains unclear. Here, we use time-resolved serial femtosecond and synchrotron crystallography to capture GTP hydrolysis in Ras crystals loaded with photoactivatable caged GTP, across timescales from milliseconds to hours. Photolysis yielded Ras in state 1—a conformation lacking a stabilized nucleophilic water characteristic of state 2. Remarkably, this state persists for hours and converts directly to Ras/GDP without passing through state 2. These findings challenge the prevailing view that state 2 is essential and suggest that state 1 can directly support catalysis, offering an alternative conceptual basis for targeting clinically relevant Ras mutants that preferentially adopt this conformation.

title: A Ferrielectric Quasi-Racemic Crystal from an Enantiopolar Racemate
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Ferrielectrics, materials with partly switchable polarization, enable functional responses such as pyroelectricity and piezoelectricity. However, general design strategies for purely organic ferrielectric crystals remain scarce. Here we show that quasiracemates (QR), derived from enantiopolar centrosymmetric racemates, may provide a novel route to organic ferrielectrics. In these structures, quasi-enantiomers assemble into antiparallel polar columns that reveal the hidden polarization of the parent racemate. We hypothesized that a quasi-enantiomer bearing an acidic proton capable of forming an additional hydrogen bond could enable ferrielectric switching. Guided by this principle, we designed a QR composed of N-Ac-R-Val and N-Ac-S-Thr. The obtained crystals exhibit P21 symmetry and display ferrielectric characteristics, along with a large absolute pyroelectric coefficient (∼3.9 × 10–9 C/(K·cm2)) and a relatively low absolute piezoelectric response (d22 ∼ 2.27 pm/V). Deuteration of the acidic protons suppresses both the large pyroelectric response and the ferrielectric switching, providing strong evidence that these phenomena are driven by these protons and their local hydrogen-bonding environment. The macroscopic polarization and polar properties are further tunable by doping N-Ac-RS-Val with varying concentrations of N-Ac-S-Thr.

title: Toward a Deeper Understanding of Single-Atom Catalysis
source: Chemical Reviews: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Single-atom catalysts (SACs) promise control of heterogeneous reactivity at a molecular level by maximizing metal utilization and enabling deliberate tuning of local coordination and microenvironment. Yet SACs expose a central challenge in modern catalysis: the catalytically relevant site is often a working-state ensemble whose coordination, charge, spin state, adsorbate binding, and environment evolve under operating conditions. As the field expands toward bimetallic motifs, atom pairs, and hybrid SAC–nanoparticle architectures, multiple site families can coexist and interconvert. This complicates unambiguous site assignment and limits general structure–property relationships. This Review offers a critical mechanistic perspective on the use of single atoms in thermal catalysis, electrocatalysis, and photocatalysis. We first summarize stabilization strategies for host matrices, emphasizing how anchoring motifs and microenvironments govern site identity and its evolution. We then develop an evidence-based approach to site assignment that treats characterization as hypothesis testing and clarifies what can and cannot be concluded regarding coordination, electronic structure, site density, and working-state identity. Finally, we connect recurring descriptors to reactivity, selectivity, and durability. We thereby highlight benchmarking techniques, site-retention metrics, and durability protocols. The goals are reliable comparison of results across studies and the transition from empirical optimization to rational design of single-atom active sites.

title: Asymmetric NIR-II Voltage-Sensitive Dyes Enable Through-Skull Single-Cell Voltage Recordings of Neurons
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Optical measurements of neuronal membrane voltage in vivo are limited by light scattering at visible wavelengths. Fluorophores operating in the second near-infrared window (NIR-II) offer improved tissue penetration; however, the reported NIR-II dyes generally lack voltage sensitivity because their dynamic symmetric structures disfavor field-sensitive charge separation. Here, we report a chemically optimized family of asymmetric NIR-II voltage-sensitive dyes. The optimized probe shows 20% fluorescence changes per 100 mV and submillisecond response kinetics, together with membrane-associated fluorescence enhancement that suppresses the background. In combination with oblique NIR-II light-sheet microscopy, the probes enable through-skull recording of spontaneous and sensory-evoked neuronal spiking at single-cell resolution in the mouse cortex at depths of ∼200–300 μm in real time, resolving fast neural spike trains. These results establish an asymmetric NIR-II fluorophore design as a route for minimally invasive optical voltage imaging in vivo.

title: Flat-band-induced integer doping and phase transition in monolayer graphene
source: Nature
abstract:
Abstract
                  
                    van der Waals heterostructures are stabilized by a delicate balance between van der Waals, elastic and Coulomb energies
                    1–4
                    . Because the interfaces are not covalently bonded, the constituent crystals can slide, rotate and reconstruct, resulting in several possible competing structural phases
                    2,5,6
                    . However, controlled tuning of this balance, and hence dynamical control over the stacking, has yet to be achieved. Here we report a dynamical heterostructure in which monolayer graphene is doubly aligned to bulk hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) and monolayer hexagonal boron nitride (mhBN) on either side. In such a system, a global structural phase transition, manifested as a change of crystalline symmetry observed by scanning tunnelling microscopy, could be induced by gating, magnetic field or temperature. This structural transition is accompanied by an exotic electronic transition: the doping of graphene switches between discrete levels, corresponding to an exact integer number of electrons or holes per moiré plaquette. We attribute this integer doping to charge trapping in localized, strain-induced pseudo-Landau levels (flat bands in reciprocal space
                    7–12
                    ), produced by moiré reconstruction (strongly enhanced by the mhBN). Electrical control of coupled structural and electronic phase transitions provides a route to engineering strain-induced flat bands and strain–Coulomb correlations in van der Waals heterostructures.

title: TransA-MERFISH reveals divergent post-retinal direction-selective circuits
source: Nature
abstract: TransA-MERFISH combines anterograde trans-neuronal tracing and spatial transcriptomics and reveals distinct retinal on–off direction-selective ganglion cell-dependent and independent motion-selective pathways in superior colliculus, establishing a sensitive cell-type-resolved framework for wiring-diagram reconstruction in early visual processing.

title: Fully integrated perovskite active polaritonic circuits
source: Nature
abstract:
Abstract
                  
                    Photonic integrated circuits are emerging as a key technology for compact, analogue and energy-efficient optical information processing
                    1
                    . Yet, their practical implementation remains limited by the intrinsically weak optical nonlinearities of conventional materials, which demand high power and large device footprints to achieve substantial nonlinear responses
                    2
                    . Exciton–polaritons, hybrid light–matter excitations of semiconducting materials, offer a promising route to overcome these limitations by combining strong optical nonlinearities with the high speed and scalability typical of photonic platforms
                    3–5
                    . However, despite their potential, fully integrated on-chip polaritonic systems simultaneously delivering room-temperature waveguide lasing, controllable optical routing and amplification have remained elusive. Here we demonstrate a fully integrated perovskite polaritonic circuit that brings these functionalities together in a single-step-grown platform. We realize precise and scalable polariton circuits with integrated gratings that act as both couplers and reflectors, enabling in-plane Fabry–Pérot cavities. These structures support robust in-plane polariton lasing with coherent guided emission at a geometry-defined wavelength, optical amplification of propagating polaritons and nonlinear optical phase control exceeding π, all within the same on-chip architecture. Our results establish perovskite polariton circuits as a scalable platform for active and interferometric integrated photonics.

title: Quantum resistance paradox of low-dimensional superfluids
source: Nature
abstract:
Abstract
                  
                    Resistance in standard conductors decreases with increasing cross-section. Yet, in low-dimensional superconductors and superfluids, residual resistance arises from topological fluctuations of the order parameter, manifesting as phase slips in one-dimensional (1D) and vortices in two-dimensional (2D) systems. How resistance and dissipation evolve as geometry interpolates between these regimes remains an open question. This evolution is masked in solid-state experiments by disorder, impurities and geometric imperfections
                    1–3
                    , and poses theoretical challenges due to competing dissipative processes and pronounced finite-size effects. Here, we use a defect-free unitary Fermi gas in a digitally programmable transport geometry to isolate geometric effects on superfluid dissipation and discover a paradox: in the crossover from one dimension to two dimensions, the resistance reaches a minimum. There, widening a channel increases its resistance. Narrower, quasi-1D channels show dissipation described by Langer–Ambegaokar–McCumber–Halperin theory of phase slips
                    4
                    . In this regime, varying the channel width yields the predicted exponential scaling of the activation factor over many orders of magnitude. Wider, quasi-2D channels show dissipation consistent with phase-slip events described by a finite-size vortex model
                    5
                    . The minimal dissipation in the dimensional crossover reflects a transition in the dominant dissipative mechanism, with both 1D and 2D events simultaneously suppressed. Our measurements suggest a route to minimizing dissipation in superconducting devices and provide a benchmark for theoretical efforts aimed at describing the dimensional crossover.

title: Analogue simulation of massive relativistic quantum fields in 2 + 1 dimensions
source: Nature
abstract:
Abstract
                  
                    Quantum field theories provide fundamental models of complex interacting systems
                    1–3
                    , from high-energy physics and cosmology to condensed matter. However, solving these models in non-perturbative and dynamical regimes is often challenging, particularly in more than one spatial dimension. Analogue simulation using tunable synthetic quantum systems can both verify existing theoretical predictions and lead to physical insights. Here we realize analogue simulation of massive relativistic quantum fields in 2 + 1 dimensions (two spatial dimensions and time), using two coherently coupled spin components
                    4,5
                    in a uniform two-dimensional atomic Bose–Einstein condensate
                    6,7
                    . Specifically, we encode the paradigmatic sine-Gordon model
                    8,9
                    in the long-wavelength modes of the field describing the relative phase,
                    ϕ
                    , of the two components. In the perturbative regime, collective field excitations exhibit a relativistic dispersion with a tunable mass gap. We also observe explicitly non-perturbative phenomena, including the existence of topological domain walls across which
                    ϕ
                    rapidly winds by 2π (ref.
                    10
                    ). Our work opens possibilities for studies of cosmologically relevant phenomena including preheating
                    11,12
                    , dynamics of topological defects
                    13,14
                    and relativistic false-vacuum decay
                    15–19
                    .

title: Bogong moths navigate with a light-dependent geomagnetic inclination compass
source: Nature
abstract:
Abstract
                  
                    Bogong moths (
                    Agrotis infusa
                    ) migrate biannually up to 1,000 km between their breeding areas and geographically restricted aestivation sites in the Australian Alps
                    1,2
                    . These moths navigate towards their distant goal using the stars as a compass
                    3
                    but navigate correctly even when the stars are obscured by clouds
                    3
                    , suggesting that their magnetic sense
                    4
                    probably harnesses the Earth’s magnetic field as a compass. However, the nature of this compass, and of the magnetic sense underlying it, remains unknown. Here we show that Bogong moths, tethered in a flight arena under a full-spectrum randomized starry night sky, navigate in their inherited migratory direction using the geomagnetic field alone. If the geomagnetic field is turned by 180°, or if inclination is inverted, moths fly in the opposite direction. If polarity is inverted, moths fail to turn. Furthermore, if violet–blue light (380 nm < 
                    λ
                     < 500 nm) is removed from the illumination spectrum, or if tethered moths are exposed to weak broadband radiofrequency fields (150 kHz to 60 MHz), magnetic orientation is abolished. Our results indicate that Bogong moths use the geomagnetic field as an inclination compass for long-distance navigation at night and possess a light-dependent radical-pair-based magnetic sense
                    5
                    .

title: Reaction‐Induced Dynamic Covalent Networking Enables Adaptive Vesicles and Hierarchical Biointerfaces
source: Advanced Materials
abstract: ABSTRACT Conventional vesicular assemblies often face challenges in balancing mechanical robustness with structural adaptability. Here, we develop a reaction‐induced dynamic covalent networking (RIDCN) strategy that integrates vesicle construction with adaptive biointerface engineering. Through the formation of interconnected imine and boronate ester linkages, RIDCN directs the assembly of non‐amphiphilic building blocks into vesicular structures, with dynamic covalent networks serving as integral membrane frameworks. This structural integration reinforces vesicle mechanics while preserving adaptive reorganization through reversible bond exchange. Beyond individual vesicles, RIDCN enables interfacial assembly on diverse implant substrates, forming adaptive coatings with antibacterial, antioxidant, immunomodulatory, and osteogenic activities. These findings demonstrate the potential of RIDCN to connect vesicle construction, mechanical adaptation, and multifunctional biointerface engineering within a unified material design strategy.

title: Metallurgical Interface Engineering Constructing In Situ Li 3 N‐Enriched Interphase: A Bulk‐Interface Synergy Strategy Toward Practical Silicon Anodes
source: Advanced Materials
abstract: ABSTRACT Silicon anodes are promising for next‐generation lithium‐ion batteries but suffer from volume expansion, unstable solid electrolyte interphase (SEI), and sluggish Li + diffusion. Herein, we report a vacuum‐suspension‐melted (VSM) bulk multiphase integration and interphase modification strategy to address these challenges. Unlike conventional mechanical mixing, VSM constructs a SiSnM (M = Bi, Ni) composite with metallurgically bonded Si/metal interfaces, forming a conductive network that buffers internal stress via atomic‐scale interfacial stress transfer. Simultaneously, a polydopamine‐derived nitrogen‐doped carbon coating transforms in situ into a Li 3 N‐enriched interphase during cycling, which exhibits high ionic/electronic conductivity, accelerates interfacial charge transfer, and suppresses continuous SEI breakdown. The resulting SiSnM@Li 3 N anode delivers 87.3% capacity retention after 1000 cycles at 1.5 A g −1 and >1000 mAh g −1 at 15 A g −1 , with reliable operation from −30°C to 60°C. Stable cycling at 2.5 mg cm −2 confirms practical relevance. Full cells with Li‐rich Mn‐based cathodes show stable performance, and 5 Ah‐level pouch cells deliver 84.7% capacity retention after 300 cycles at 6 A discharge. This work concurrently tackles ionic, electronic, and mechanical constraints, offering a practical path to high‐energy durable Si‐based batteries.

title: Probing Electron-Spin Redistribution in Trimetallic FeMoFe Complexes
source: Journal of the American Chemical Society: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract The cooperative interplay between iron and molybdenum in modulating electron-spin effects for small-molecule activation remains a fundamental challenge in bioinorganic chemistry. Here we report a trimetallic FeMoFe platform that captures this synergy across two accessible redox levels: 1+ ([Fe2+Mo3+Fe2+], S = 1/2) and 12+ ([Fe2+Mo4+Fe2+], S = 0). Comprehensive spectroscopic and electronic structure analysis reveals that 1+ adopts a partially delocalized configuration comprising an intermediate-spin Fe2+ (S = 1), a low-spin Fe2+ (S = 0), and a low-spin Mo3+ (S = 1/2) center, which couple to afford an overall S = 1/2 ground state. One-electron oxidation of 1+ to 12+ triggers a profound intramolecular electron redistribution, wherein the molybdenum functions as a redox buffer that equilibrates local electron density, yielding a [Fe2+Mo4+Fe2+] configuration with two S = 1 ferrous sites antiferromagnetically coupled. This adaptive electronic flexibility is manifested in two distinct reactivity pathways: CO binding to 1+ drives a change in the local spin state of one Fe center, yielding an S = 1/2 symmetric [(CO)Fe2+Mo3+Fe2+(CO)]+ complex having two low-spin Fe2+ sites; conversely, 12+ harnesses the electron-spin effects at each Fe2+ site to accomplish the two-electron reductive cleavage of N2H4, affording a rare example of diferric diamido complex, [(NH2)Fe3+Mo4+Fe3+(NH2)]2+ (S = 0).

title: Anodic Selective Etching: A Mechanism‐Centric Perspective for Electrochemical Subtractive Manufacturing
source: Advanced Materials
abstract: ABSTRACT Anodic selective etching (ASE) is a precision electrochemical subtractive manufacturing strategy that enables controllable material removal, interfacial reconstruction, and morphology evolution under electrochemically controlled conditions. Unlike material‐centric reviews that mainly catalogue substrates or products, this mechanism‐centric framework reveals common electrochemical principles, enabling cross‐material comparison, transferable design rules, and predictive control over selectivity, reaction location, and structural evolution. This review unifies ASE across material platforms and structural scales through five dominant modes: composition‐ and phase‐selective anodic dissolution, structural site‐selective anodic etching, semiconductor carrier‐ and space‐charge‐controlled etching, film‐ and passivation‐controlled subtraction, and geometry‐ or three‐phase boundary‐localized etching, together with representative coupled mechanisms. The roles of anodic material characteristics, electrolyte composition, and electrochemical parameters in defining selectivity windows, localization behavior, and structural outcomes are critically discussed. These mechanisms enable low‐dimensional materials, porous and core–shell architectures, surface finishing and shaping, and meniscus‐localized tip fabrication. Key challenges in multicomponent selectivity, electrolyte sustainability, and scalable manufacturing are outlined, alongside opportunities in in situ and operando characterization, multi‐physics modeling, and data‐driven optimization toward reproducible and programmable electrochemical manufacturing.

title: Single-atom catalyst–Li2O2 interfacial chemistry governs the activity–stability trade-off in Li–O2 batteries
source: National Science Review Advance Access
abstract: Cathode catalysts in aprotic Li–O2 batteries are commonly judged by their ability to lower charge overpotentials, yet improved catalytic activity often does not lead to durable cycling. Here, we use structurally well-defined M–N4 single-atom catalysts (SACs) as model cathodes to elucidate the interplay between catalyst activity and battery stability. Integrated experimental and theoretical studies suggest that, although SACs promote Li2O2 oxidation and lower the initial charging overpotential, they also increase the reactivity of discharge-generated Li2O2 toward ether electrolytes, promoting carboxylate accumulation and cathode passivation. On the basis of this mechanistic insight, a localized high-concentration electrolyte is introduced to regulate the catalyst–Li2O2 interfacial chemistry, suppress side reactions, and extend the cycling life from 42 to 398 cycles. This work identifies a previously overlooked trade-off between catalytic activity and battery stability in Li–O2 batteries and provides a mechanistic foundation for designing stable catalyst/electrolyte interfaces in high-energy electrochemical devices.

title: Tropical land-use intensification restructures biodiversity
source: Nature
abstract:
Abstract
                  
                    Tropical land-use intensification threatens global biodiversity, yet most assessments of tropical agricultural landscapes focus on local-scale biodiversity, overlooking how land use restructures biodiversity across space and multiple taxa. Here we provide an ecosystem-wide assessment of 24 taxonomic groups across all domains of life—encompassing 40,049 species—along a land-use intensification gradient from lowland forests to intensively managed smallholder cash-crop monocultures in Indonesian landscapes. Despite widespread losses of landscape and local multidiversity
                    1
                    in monocultures (approximately 78% and 50%, respectively), we found no evidence for consistent community homogenization with land-use intensification. Instead, monocultures exhibit a systematic shift from turnover to nestedness for aboveground taxa. Such patterns of differentiation may mask trajectories towards biotic homogenization via early stages of assemblage simplification. Biotic differentiation has the potential to partly mitigate biodiversity losses by positively affecting γ-diversity. This opens management options, including the conservation of existing remnants of traditional agriculture and the implementation of sustainable management practices
                    2–4
                    . Our results demonstrate that tropical land-use intensification restructures biodiversity not only through species loss, but also via a pervasive reorganization of community composition across trophic levels. Conserving tropical biodiversity, therefore, requires a multi-taxon, landscape-scale perspective that explicitly integrates agricultural land uses with the protection of natural and semi-natural habitats to reconcile agricultural production and conservation.

title: Evidence for p-wave magnetism in electronic band structure of metallic EuSi
source: Nature
abstract:
Abstract
                  
                    One active frontier of quantum-matter research is the realization of
                    p
                    -wave symmetry-breaking phases in fermionic systems, long exemplified by the A phase of superfluid helium-3 (refs.
                    1–3
                    ). Achieving
                    p
                    -wave superconductivity
                    4
                    and its magnetic analogue
                    5
                    —characterized by a time-reversal-symmetric,
                    p
                    -wave spin-polarized Fermi surface—remains a grand challenge
                    6,7
                    . Despite recent progress in identifying candidate
                    p
                    -wave magnets
                    5,7–10
                    , spin-resolved spectroscopic evidence for their electronic structures remains limited. Here we report angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES) and spin-ARPES evidence for
                    p
                    -wave magnetism in the near-Fermi-level electronic structure of stoichiometric metallic EuSi, supported by symmetry analysis, first-principles calculations and neutron scattering. Neutron diffraction reveals a chiral spiral phase between 33.4 K and 62 K that fulfils archetypal
                    p
                    -wave magnetism criteria: it preserves the combined symmetry of time reversal and lattice translation, while breaking inversion symmetry. Spin-integrated ARPES reveals a pronounced magnetism-driven reconstruction of the electronic structure, with energy separations exceeding 100 meV, and spin-ARPES resolves
                    S
                    
                      y
                    
                    polarization in near-Fermi-level spectral features. The extracted
                    S
                    
                      y
                    
                    exhibits a sign-changing modulation across successive magnetic Brillouin zones and is suppressed near the nodal regions, consistent with the predicted
                    p
                    -wave spin texture and unfolded spin-polarization calculations. Magnetic force microscopy and micro-ARPES further reveal approximately 10-μm chiral magnetic domains. These results identify EuSi as a stoichiometric metallic platform for investigating
                    p
                    -wave magnetism in electronic band structures and spin-symmetry-based functionalities in spintronics
                    10
                    , topological matter
                    7
                    , superconductivity
                    11
                    and beyond.

title: Closest relatives of poxviruses prevail in human and animal guts worldwide
source: Nature
abstract:
Abstract
                  
                    Large and giant double-stranded DNA viruses substantially affect eukaryotic ecology and evolution
                    1–4
                    . They prevail in the environment but are rarely found in the digestive system of animals
                    5,6
                    . Here we present the discovery of a diversified group of DNA viruses with large linear genomes, dubbed egoviruses, that comprise a putative viral order most closely related to animal-infecting poxviruses. Egoviruses are found worldwide, almost exclusively in the digestive system of humans, livestock and wild animals. The most prevalent human-specific egovirus is spread across continents, demonstrating a long-term association between egoviruses and the human gut microbiome. Eukaryotic homologues of egovirus core genes suggest that these viruses primarily infect Trichostomatia (ciliates), which assist ruminant digestive processes
                    7
                    , and Parabasalia (Metamonada), which influence animal immunity and gut microbiome ecology
                    8
                    . Egoviruses also contributed to the genetic makeup of polintons, endogenous viruses that proliferated in genomes of
                    Trichomonas
                    vaginalis
                    9
                    and its close Parabasalia relatives. Unlike poxviruses that form brick-shaped virions, egoviruses are predicted to form multilayered icosahedral capsids resembling those of asfuviruses and probably representing the ancestral virion structure. Egoviruses are the only known clade of double-stranded DNA viruses of eukaryotes prevailing in the animal digestive system. Phylogenomic analysis suggests an evolutionary scenario whereby egovirus-like ancestors of poxviruses infected anaerobic unicellular eukaryotes inside the gut of ancestral animals, before transitioning to animal cell infection, which was accompanied by the virion metamorphosis.

title: Structural and regulatory evolution across the genus Hordeum
source: Nature
abstract:
Abstract
                  
                    The genus
                    Hordeum
                    comprises cultivated barley and its wild relatives, an evolutionarily, ecologically and agriculturally important group of grasses
                    1,2
                    . Here we generated a chromosome-scale comparative genomic resource comprising all recognized diploid
                    Hordeum
                    species together with representative polyploid lineages. Comparative analyses reveal extensive structural variation, including inversions and chromosomal rearrangements that disrupt proximal collinearity and reflect lineage-specific genome remodelling. Single-copy gene phylogenies identify ancient hybridization, segmental exchange and introgression, revealing pervasive reticulate evolution during
                    Hordeum
                    diversification. We uncover widespread horizontal gene transfer from Panicoideae grasses into
                    Hordeum
                    , with many transferred genes showing evidence of transcription and functional integration. Retrotransposon proliferation explains genome size variation and provides insights into polyploid genome evolution. Whole-genome alignments reveal contrasting evolutionary dynamics: whereas coding sequences remain highly conserved, regulatory elements undergo rapid turnover, providing a rich source of regulatory diversity for phenotypic evolution. Case studies of vernalization and glume development demonstrate how natural variation in regulatory and coding sequences contributes to flowering time and floral morphology. This comprehensive pangenomic framework establishes
                    Hordeum
                    as a model for studying genome evolution, structural variation and the genetic basis of adaptive traits, offering new avenues for barley improvement.

title: Injury-induced signalling coordinates immunity and cannibalism in locusts
source: Nature
abstract:
Abstract
                  
                    Cannibalism, the consumption of conspecifics, is widespread across the animal kingdom and can profoundly influence individual fitness and population dynamics
                    1,2
                    . Although the ecological and social conditions that favour cannibalism have been well documented
                    2
                    , the molecular signals that trigger cannibalistic attacks have remained poorly understood. Here we show that in
                    Locusta migratoria
                    , guaiacol, a volatile compound with augmented release after injury, attracts gregarious nymphs and induces cannibalistic behaviour. Guaiacol is detected by olfactory receptors LmOR36 and LmOR34, and disruption of either receptor abolishes attraction, thereby impairing induction of cannibalism. Guaiacol is synthesized by haemolymph symbiont
                    Enterobacter hormaechei
                    . Injury promotes bacterial congregation at the wound site, leading to elevated guaiacol production through a clustered set of vanillic acid decarboxylase genes; deletion of this gene cluster abolishes guaiacol production and its behavioural effects. Notably, guaiacol initially functions as a beneficial signal after injury. Guaiacol activates immune-related pathways in wounded locusts, enhancing pathogen resistance and increasing survival following minor injury. However, when guaiacol emission exceeds a threshold determined by injury severity, it functions as an external cue that attracts cannibals. Cannibalistic locusts exploit this immune-related odour to locate severely injured conspecifics, gaining both nutritional resources and immune system benefits. Together, our findings identify a microbial–chemical mechanism that links immune defence with cannibalistic behaviour and provide potential molecular targets for manipulation of cannibalism-dependent population dynamics.

title: Ferroptosis in cancer cells triggers PGE2 production for tumour immune escape
source: Nature
abstract:
Abstract
                  
                    Ferroptosis, a form of cell death induced by overwhelming membrane lipid peroxidation, is a vulnerability of many cancers, including cancers resistant to current molecular and immune-based therapies
                    1–7
                    . Triggering of ferroptosis therefore provides an opportunity to achieve elimination of difficult-to-treat cancers
                    1–4,8,9
                    . Studies in mouse cancer models have demonstrated that anticancer immunity, mediated by dendritic cells (DCs) and CD8
                    +
                    T cells, is essential for effective tumour eradication by ferroptosis-inducing strategies
                    10–13
                    . However, ferroptotic cells limit this response
                    8–10,14
                    , resulting in immune escape and tumour growth through mechanisms that remain unclear. Here we demonstrate that ferroptotic cancer cells activate a molecular program resulting in aberrant production of prostaglandin E
                    2
                    (PGE
                    2
                    ), which limits the stimulation of anticancer CD8
                    +
                    T cell responses by type 1 conventional DCs (cDC1s), thereby promoting immune escape. In ferroptotic cancer cells, lipid peroxidation-mediated membrane permeabilization enables Ca
                    2+
                    influx, which activates p38 MAPK signalling and thereby drives PGE
                    2
                    production. This signalling axis is uncoupled from cancer cell death and can be targeted to selectively interfere with immune-inhibitory PGE
                    2
                    production while preserving ferroptotic cancer cell elimination. In the context of cancer cell ferroptosis, ablation of PGE
                    2
                    production or disrupting PGE
                    2
                    signalling restores cDC1-mediated anticancer CD8
                    +
                    T cell responses and leads to effective tumour elimination. Our findings identify a key mechanism that limits antitumour immunity and prevents tumour elimination upon ferroptosis induction in cancer cells, which could be exploited for cancer therapy.

title: Band-Edge-Extended Heterointerfaces for Perovskite Solar Cells and Tandems
source: Nature
abstract: Perovskite solar cells (PSCs) have emerged as a promising photovoltaic technology, with efficiencies rapidly approaching those of established crystalline-silicon solar cells. Further efficiency gains, however, are increasingly limited by charge extraction and recombination at the interface between the perovskite absorber and the electron-transport layer. Interfacial modifiers are widely used to suppress these losses, yet many conventional ammonium-based modifiers are weakly electronically coupled to the perovskite surface and can introduce barriers to electron extraction 1-5. Here we realize electronically coupled heterointerfaces by introducing a family of heteroatom-containing, fully conjugated formamidinium interfacial modulators, establishing band-edge-extending conjugated heterointerfaces that overcome the bottleneck of inefficient interfacial electron transfer. The resulting band-edge-extended heterointerface establishes delocalized electron connectivity at the perovskite/electron transporting layer (ETL) interface and suppresses interfacial non-radiative recombination. We report a certified power-conversion efficiency (PCE) of 27.96% and a stabilized power output (SPO) of 27.84% for inverted PSCs. The corresponding devices retained over 95% of their initial efficiency after 2000 h continuous maximum-power-point tracking under 1-sun irradiation (ISOS-L). Extending this strategy to monolithic perovskite–silicon tandems enables a certified SPO of 34.71%, establishing band-edge extension as a broadly applicable approach to overcoming the conventional trade-off between interfacial passivation and charge extraction.

title: Architected Si-Based Anodes for All-Solid-State Lithium Batteries
source: ACS Energy Letters: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Silicon anodes have emerged as a key enabler for next-generation all-solid-state batteries (ASSBs). In particular, the Li-Si alloy shows a low expansion coefficient and high ionic/electronic conductivity, but remains plagued by poor mechanical integrity and interfacial stability. Here we describe a Mg-doped Si interlayer at the Li metal-Li6PS5Cl interface, which electrochemically transforms into a Li-rich composite anode comprising Li14.39Mg0.61Si4 and Li-Mg alloy during cycling. Mg incorporation promotes the formation of a homogeneous lithiated Si framework, establishing a continuous ion/electron transport network. In addition, the unique porous architecture effectively mitigates stress and achieves favorable mechanical matching with Li6PS5Cl, thereby enhancing structural stability. Paired with a LiNi0.8Co0.1Mn0.1O2 cathode, the cell with an areal loading of 17.9 mg cm–2 delivers stable cycling over 1000 cycles at 3 C with 92.5% capacity retention. This multicomponent anode design offers a new paradigm for structural engineering of Si-based anodes and paves the way for high-energy-density ASSBs.

title: Controllable Growth of Micron-Thick Films for Bifacial Perovskite Solar Cells
source: ACS Energy Letters: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract Bifacial perovskite solar cells require a micron-thick absorber layer to compensate for optical losses, yet the poor controllability in fabricating high-quality thick films critically limits device performance. Here, we developed an isopropyl alcohol (IPA) vapor atmosphere control system. By precisely tuning the duration of N2 purging to introduce IPA vapor into the PbI2 annealing chamber, we obtained a porous, highly crystalline PbI2–IPA intermediate film that facilitates subsequent ammonium salt intercalation. This results in a substantially lower energy barrier for the conversion from PbI2–IPA to α-FAPbI3, enabling the spontaneous α-phase formation at room temperature while completely bypassing the undesirable δ-phase. The resulting bifacial PSCs achieve a high power conversion efficiency of 23.78% (certified 23.71%) and a power generation density of 27.83 mW/cm2 with a short-circuit current density of 29.96 mA/cm2, at an albedo of 0.2, demonstrating excellent performance for bifacial PSCs. This work provides a rational pathway toward efficient bifacial perovskite photovoltaics.

title: Impacts of Residence Time and Temperature on CO Electrolysis to Acetate at the 100 cm2 Electrode Scale
source: ACS Energy Letters: Latest Articles (ACS Publications)
abstract: Abstract The electrochemical reduction of carbon monoxide (CO) to acetate offers a promising route to upgrade waste carbon into a valuable product, yet scale-up beyond laboratory-scale cells remains underexplored. Here, we develop a 100 cm2 CO electrolyzer in a membrane–electrode assembly (MEA) configuration using a computational fluid dynamics (CFD)-guided approach. An anode-side serpentine flow field increases electrolyte velocity and anolyte residence time, facilitating oxygen removal and promoting further anodic oxidation of crossover ethanol to acetate. Combined with controlled reactor temperature, these effects improve acetate selectivity and operational stability. At 200 mA cm–2, the electrolyzer achieves a peak acetate Faradaic efficiency (FE) of 65% and stable operation for 140 h. These results identify anolyte residence time and reactor temperature as important reactor-level parameters impacting product distribution and stability, providing practical design guidance for selective and scalable CO-to-acetate electrolysis at the 100 cm2 scale.
